    41	For an admissible tuple $(q,m,d)$ and a strategy that wins the Pauli basis test
    42	with probability at least $1-\eps$, each subtest has conditional failure
    43	$O(\eps)$.  In particular, the Magic Square average is conditioned on
    44	\[
    45	  \gamma(\omega)
    46	  =\tr\big((r_X\ind_m(u_X))\cdot(r_Z\ind_m(u_Z))\big)\ne0,
    47	\]
    48	and the low-degree line-evaluation family is completed on zero-direction lines
    49	by an additional outcome.  The observable consequence is
    50	\[
    51	  X^{r_X}(u_X)Z^{r_Z}(u_Z)
    52	  \approx_{\sqrt\eps}
    53	  (-1)^{\gamma(\omega)}Z^{r_Z}(u_Z)X^{r_X}(u_X)
    54	\]
    55	on average over all tuples.  These statements hold for every admissible
    56	parameter tuple; no assumption $6md\leq q$ is needed.
    57	
    58	\section{The source assertions and discrepancies}
    59	
    60	The source states the measurement implications at lines~197--265 and the
    61	observable implications at lines~267--362 of the Pauli analysis
    62	\cite[lines~197--362]{Ji2020MIPStar}.%
    63	\footnote{See
    64	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex}.}
    65	Four corrections are required.
    66	
    67	First, the displayed conditioning event for the Magic Square average omits
    68	$\ind_m$ and writes the scalar expression
    69	$\tr((r_Xu_X)\cdot(r_Zu_Z))$, even though $u_X,u_Z\in\F_q^m$ and the phase
    70	used by the game is defined through vectors in $\F_q^{2^m}$.
    71	
    72	Second, the proof assumes $6md\leq q$ and disposes of the complementary range
    73	by appealing to the final Pauli soundness theorem, whose proof uses the lemma
    74	under discussion.  That appeal cannot prove the lemma as an unrestricted
    75	standalone result.  The corrected exact probability calculation gives
    76	universal lower bounds for both conditioning events whenever the parameters
    77	are admissible, and removes this circular reduction.%
    78	\footnote{The probability correction is documented separately in
    79	\path{docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_anticommuting-probability.tex}.}
    80	
    81	Third, the source treats evaluation classes of a line measurement as a POVM
    82	indexed by $\F_q$.  A zero-direction line admits nonconstant polynomial
    83	representatives with no well-defined value on its singleton image, so these
    84	classes form only a sub-measurement.  Adding an outcome $\bot$ for the missing
    85	mass makes the consistency relation well typed; the point family is completed
    86	by a zero effect at the same outcome.
    87	
    88	Finally, the observable proof writes
    89	$Z^{r_X}(u_X)X^{r_Z}(u_Z)$ where the intended reversed product is
    90	$Z^{r_Z}(u_Z)X^{r_X}(u_X)$.  The source label prefix
    91	\path{len:qld-win-implications-obs} is likewise a typographical error for
    92	\path{lem:qld-win-implications-obs}.
    93	
    94	\section{The corrected argument}
    95	
    96	Every question type and every relevant subtest has a universal positive
    97	sampling weight.  For admissible parameters, $1\leq m\leq q$, and the exact
    98	calculation of the anticommuting probability gives probability at least
    99	$2^{-4}$ for the anticommuting event and at least $1/2$ for its complement.
   100	Conditioning therefore enlarges rejection probabilities only by a universal
   101	factor.  The measurement implications follow directly from their rejection
   102	events, including the completed zero-direction outcome.  Data processing and
   103	the agreement identities yield the observable relations; the corrected Magic
   104	Square phase and reversed product then give the displayed signed commutation
   105	law.
   106	
   107	\section{Blueprint and formalization status}
   108	
   109	The blueprint uses the full phase $\gamma$, completes the line-evaluation
   110	families, proves the conditioning step with the universal probability bounds,
   111	and corrects the reversed product and label.  Its proof and correction remark
   112	cite this note.  The linked formal declarations use the same conditional
   113	distributions and completed line outcomes, so their statements agree with the
   114	corrected blueprint.  Their proofs remain open in the current tree.%
   115	\footnote{The relevant declarations are \leanid{win\_cons},
   116	\leanid{win\_low\_degree}, \leanid{win\_pauli\_basis\_cons},
   117	\leanid{win\_comm}, \leanid{win\_comm\_cons},
   118	\leanid{win\_magic\_square}, \leanid{win\_ms\_cons}, and their
   119	\path{\_approx} companions in
   120	\doclink{MIPStarRE/QPBT/Observables/WinImplications.lean}.}
   121	
   122	\section{Conclusion}
   123	
   124	The winning implications remain valid for all admissible parameters, but the
   125	printed proof does not establish that scope and several formulas need local
   126	correction.  Exact conditioning probabilities, the explicit missing outcome,
   127	and the corrected phase and operator indices give the form used by the Pauli
   128	basis analysis.

    21	\section{At a glance}
    22	
    23	\begin{itemize}
    24	  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Low.  A product expansion computes the
    25	  probability exactly and exposes two false claims in the printed proof.
    26	  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} The formal correction consists of one
    27	  finite-field counting theorem and elementary real inequalities, roughly
    28	  100--180 lines.
    29	  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} About 40\% finite counting and real
    30	  inequalities, and 60\% project-local finite-field coordinates and sampling.
    31	  \item \textbf{Key Mathlib inputs.} Uniform finite distributions, field-trace
    32	  fibers, Bernoulli's inequality, and the fixed self-dual basis.  The formal
    33	  proof is tracked in \ghissue{110}.
    34	\end{itemize}
    35	
    36	\section{Key theorem forms}
    37	
    38	Let $q=2^k$, let $u_X,u_Z$ be uniform in $\F_q^m$, and let $r_X,r_Z$ be
    39	uniform in $\F_q$.  Put
    40	\[
    41	  \gamma=\tr\big((r_X\ind_m(u_X))\cdot(r_Z\ind_m(u_Z))\big).
    42	\]
    43	Then
    44	\[
    45	  \Pr[\gamma\ne0]=\frac12(1-q^{-1})^{m+1},
    46	  \qquad
    47	  \Pr[\gamma=0]\geq\frac12.
    48	\]
    49	In particular, $m\leq q$ gives the uniform lower bound
    50	$\Pr[\gamma\ne0]\geq2^{-4}$.  If $m,d\geq1$, the two lower bounds printed in
    51	the source also hold:
    52	\[
    53	  \Pr[\gamma\ne0]
    54	  \geq \frac12(1-q^{-m})(1-q^{-1})(1-md/q)
    55	  \geq \frac12(1-3md/q),
    56	\]
    57	and $\Pr[\gamma=0]\geq\frac12(1-3md/q)$.
    58	
    59	\section{The source assertion and discrepancy}
    60	
    61	Fact \path{fact:omega-anticomm-prob} of the Pauli analysis
    62	\cite[lines~64--93]{Ji2020MIPStar} states the last two bounds without the
    63	positivity assumptions on $m$ and $d$.  Its proof starts by
    64	asserting that $\ind_m(u_X)=0$ if and only if $u_X=0$, and that $u_X=0$ forces
    65	$\gamma=0$.%
    66	\footnote{See
    67	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex},
    68	lines~64--93.}
    69	Both assertions are false.  The coordinates of $\ind_m(u)$ sum to one, so the
    70	indicator vector never vanishes.  For $(q,m,d)=(2,1,0)$ and
    71	$(u_X,u_Z,r_X,r_Z)=(0,0,1,1)$, the phase is nonzero.  In the same parameter
    72	case the exact anticommuting probability is $1/8$, below the printed lower
    73	bound $1/2$.  Thus the missing hypothesis $d\geq1$ is mathematically necessary
    74	for that displayed bound.
    75	
    76	\section{The corrected calculation}
    77	
    78	In characteristic two, expansion over the Boolean cube gives
    79	\[
    80	  \ind_m(u_X)\cdot\ind_m(u_Z)
    81	  =\prod_{i=1}^m(1+u_{X,i}+u_{Z,i}).
    82	\]
    83	For fixed $u_X$, the factors are independent and uniform as $u_Z$ varies, so
    84	they are all nonzero with probability $(1-q^{-1})^m$.  Independently,
    85	$r_X\ne0$ with probability $1-q^{-1}$.  Conditioned on these events, the
    86	argument of the trace is uniform as $r_Z$ varies, and a nonzero linear trace
    87	to $\F_2$ takes the value one with probability $1/2$.  This proves the exact
    88	formula.  Bernoulli's inequality gives the stated source bounds when
    89	$m,d\geq1$; the admissible Pauli-test parameters satisfy these conditions.
    90	
    91	\section{Blueprint and formalization status}
    92	
    93	The blueprint states the exact probability, restores $m,d\geq1$ on the
    94	source bounds, and uses the unconditional constant lower bound when
    95	conditioning the winning implications.  Its proof and correction remark cite
    96	this note.  The corresponding formal declarations have the same corrected
    97	statements, but their proofs remain open in the current tree.%
    98	\footnote{The declarations are \leanid{anticommProb\_eq},
    99	\leanid{commProb\_ge\_half}, \leanid{anticommProb\_ge\_of\_m\_le\_q}, and
   100	\leanid{anticommProb\_ge\_of\_one\_le\_md} in
   101	\doclink{MIPStarRE/QPBT/Observables/Anticommuting.lean}.}
   102	
   103	\section{Conclusion}
   104	
   105	The source proof is incorrect, and its displayed bound fails when $d=0$.
   106	The exact probability is $\frac12(1-q^{-1})^{m+1}$.  It yields universal
   107	conditioning probabilities for all admissible parameters and recovers the
   108	printed lower bounds after making the implicit positivity assumptions explicit.

     3	/-!
     4	# Commuting and anticommuting Pauli tuples
     5	
     6	This module defines the tuple phase used in the Pauli basis test and the
     7	conditional uniform distributions used by its observable analysis.
     8	
     9	## References
    10	
    11	The definitions and probability bounds formalize `def:anticommuting-tuple`
    12	and `fact:omega-anticomm-prob` in
    13	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:128-267`, with paper origin
    14	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:64-95`.
    15	-/
    16	
    17	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    18	
    19	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    20	
    21	noncomputable section
    22	
    23	/-- A tuple `(u_X,u_Z,r_X,r_Z)` over the fixed field model of an admissible
    24	Pauli-test parameter tuple. This is the tuple space of
    25	`def:anticommuting-tuple`, blueprint `ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:128-148`, paper
    26	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:64-68`. -/
    27	abbrev PauliTuple (P : AdmissibleParams) :=
    28	  (Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) ×
    29	    (Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) × PauliScalar P × PauliScalar P
    30	
    31	/-- A Pauli tuple is anticommuting when its phase bit is nonzero. This is
    32	`def:anticommuting-tuple`, blueprint `ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:128-148`, paper
    33	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:64-68`. -/
    34	def IsAnticommuting {P : AdmissibleParams} (ω : PauliTuple P) : Prop :=
    35	  gammaValue P ω.1 ω.2.1 ω.2.2.1 ω.2.2.2 ≠ 0

    22	
    23	\begin{itemize}

    31	  \item \textbf{Key Mathlib inputs.} Uniform finite distributions, field-trace

    36	\section{Key theorem forms}
    37	
    38	Let $q=2^k$, let $u_X,u_Z$ be uniform in $\F_q^m$, and let $r_X,r_Z$ be
    39	uniform in $\F_q$.  Put
    40	\[
    41	  \gamma=\tr\big((r_X\ind_m(u_X))\cdot(r_Z\ind_m(u_Z))\big).
    42	\]
    43	Then
    44	\[
    45	  \Pr[\gamma\ne0]=\frac12(1-q^{-1})^{m+1},
    46	  \qquad
    47	  \Pr[\gamma=0]\geq\frac12.
    48	\]
    49	In particular, $m\leq q$ gives the uniform lower bound
    50	$\Pr[\gamma\ne0]\geq2^{-4}$.  If $m,d\geq1$, the two lower bounds printed in
    51	the source also hold:
    52	\[
    53	  \Pr[\gamma\ne0]
    54	  \geq \frac12(1-q^{-m})(1-q^{-1})(1-md/q)
    55	  \geq \frac12(1-3md/q),
    56	\]
    57	and $\Pr[\gamma=0]\geq\frac12(1-3md/q)$.
    58	
    59	\section{The source assertion and discrepancy}
    60	
    61	Fact \path{fact:omega-anticomm-prob} of the Pauli analysis
    62	\cite[lines~64--93]{Ji2020MIPStar} states the last two bounds without the
    63	positivity assumptions on $m$ and $d$.  Its proof starts by
    64	asserting that $\ind_m(u_X)=0$ if and only if $u_X=0$, and that $u_X=0$ forces
    65	$\gamma=0$.%
    66	\footnote{See
    67	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex},
    68	lines~64--93.}
    69	Both assertions are false.  The coordinates of $\ind_m(u)$ sum to one, so the
    70	indicator vector never vanishes.  For $(q,m,d)=(2,1,0)$ and
    71	$(u_X,u_Z,r_X,r_Z)=(0,0,1,1)$, the phase is nonzero.  In the same parameter
    72	case the exact anticommuting probability is $1/8$, below the printed lower
    73	bound $1/2$.  Thus the missing hypothesis $d\geq1$ is mathematically necessary
    74	for that displayed bound.
    75	
    76	\section{The corrected calculation}
    77	
    78	In characteristic two, expansion over the Boolean cube gives
    79	\[
    80	  \ind_m(u_X)\cdot\ind_m(u_Z)
    81	  =\prod_{i=1}^m(1+u_{X,i}+u_{Z,i}).
    82	\]
    83	For fixed $u_X$, the factors are independent and uniform as $u_Z$ varies, so
    84	they are all nonzero with probability $(1-q^{-1})^m$.  Independently,
    85	$r_X\ne0$ with probability $1-q^{-1}$.  Conditioned on these events, the
    86	argument of the trace is uniform as $r_Z$ varies, and a nonzero linear trace
    87	to $\F_2$ takes the value one with probability $1/2$.  This proves the exact
    88	formula.  Bernoulli's inequality gives the stated source bounds when
    89	$m,d\geq1$; the admissible Pauli-test parameters satisfy these conditions.
    90	
    91	\section{Blueprint and formalization status}
    92	
    93	The blueprint states the exact probability, restores $m,d\geq1$ on the
    94	source bounds, and uses the unconditional constant lower bound when
    95	conditioning the winning implications.  Its proof and correction remark cite
    96	this note.  The corresponding formal declarations have the same corrected
    97	statements, but their proofs remain open in the current tree.%
    98	\footnote{The declarations are \leanid{anticommProb\_eq},
    99	\leanid{commProb\_ge\_half}, \leanid{anticommProb\_ge\_of\_m\_le\_q}, and
   100	\leanid{anticommProb\_ge\_of\_one\_le\_md} in
   101	\doclink{MIPStarRE/QPBT/Observables/Anticommuting.lean}.}
   102	
   103	\section{Conclusion}
   104	
   105	The source proof is incorrect, and its displayed bound fails when $d=0$.
   106	The exact probability is $\frac12(1-q^{-1})^{m+1}$.  It yields universal
   107	conditioning probabilities for all admissible parameters and recovers the
   108	printed lower bounds after making the implicit positivity assumptions explicit.

   159	\begin{lemma}[Probability of anticommuting tuples]
   160		\label{fact:omega-anticomm-prob}
   161		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.anticommProb, MIPStarRE.QPBT.anticommProb_eq}
   162		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.commProb, MIPStarRE.QPBT.commProb_ge_half}
   163		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.anticommProb_ge_of_m_le_q}
   164		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.anticommProb_ge_of_one_le_md}
   165		\leanok
   166		% The source states this result in a `fact' environment; it is stated here
   167		% as a lemma, and the paper label is kept verbatim.
   168		% The exact value of the anticommuting probability and the constant lower
   169		% bounds under the hypothesis m <= q are additions relative to the source,
   170		% which asserts only the two bounds displayed at the end of the statement;
   171		% the source states those bounds without the hypothesis m, d >= 1, under
   172		% which alone they hold (see the remark following this lemma). The
   173		% unconditional constant bounds are what the proof of the lemma labelled
   174		% lem:qld-win-implications uses.
   175		\uses{def:anticommuting-tuple}
   176		A tuple $\omega = (u_X,u_Z,r_X,r_Z)$ sampled uniformly at random from
   177		$(\F_q^m)^2 \times (\F_q)^2$ is anticommuting with probability exactly
   178		\[
   179			\big(1 - q^{-1}\big)^{m+1} \cdot \frac{1}{2}\,,
   180		\]
   181		and commuting with the complementary probability, which is at least
   182		$\frac12$. In particular, if $m \leq q$, then $\omega$ is anticommuting
   183		with probability at least $2^{-4}$ and commuting with probability at
   184		least $\frac12$. If $m, d \geq 1$, then the probability that $\omega$ is
   185		anticommuting is at least
   186		\[
   187			(1 - q^{-m}) \cdot (1 - q^{-1}) \cdot \Big(1 - \frac{md}{q}\Big) \cdot \frac{1}{2}
   188			\,\geq\, \Big(1 - \frac{3md}{q}\Big) \cdot \frac{1}{2}\,,
   189		\]
   190		and the probability that $\omega$ is commuting is also at least
   191		$\big(1 - \frac{3md}{q}\big) \cdot \frac{1}{2}$.  These corrections are
   192		documented in \cite{gap:qpbt_anticommuting-probability}.
   193	\end{lemma}
   194	\begin{proof}
   195		\uses{def:low-degree-encoding, def:indicator-vector, def:admissible-size, def:binary-representation, lem:downsize_field, lem:one}
   196		By the definition of the indicator vector
   197		(Definition~\ref{def:indicator-vector}), expanding the product over the
   198		coordinates $i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ into a sum over $y \in \{0,1\}^m$
   199		gives
   200		\[
   201			\mathrm{ind}_m(u_X) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_Z)
   202			\,=\, \sum_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} \mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(u_X)\, \mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(u_Z)
   203			\,=\, \prod_{i=1}^{m} \big( u_{X,i}\, u_{Z,i} + (1 - u_{X,i})(1 - u_{Z,i}) \big)\,,
   204		\]
   205		and since $\F_q$ has characteristic $2$, the $i$-th factor equals
   206		$1 + u_{X,i} + u_{Z,i}$. Hence
   207		\[
   208			\gamma(\omega) \,=\, \tr\Big( (r_X r_Z) \cdot \prod_{i=1}^{m} (1 + u_{X,i} + u_{Z,i}) \Big)\,.
   209		\]
   210		For any fixed $u_X$, the $m$ factors $1 + u_{X,i} + u_{Z,i}$ are
   211		independent and uniformly distributed in $\F_q$ over the choice of
   212		$u_Z$, so all of them are nonzero with probability $(1-q^{-1})^m$;
   213		independently, $r_X \neq 0$ with probability $1 - q^{-1}$. If $r_X = 0$
   214		or some factor vanishes, then $\gamma(\omega) = 0$. Otherwise, over the
   215		uniform choice of $r_Z$, the argument of the trace is a uniformly random
   216		element of $\F_q$. Since $q = 2^k$ is admissible, the trace of an
   217		element of $\F_q$ equals the coordinate sum of its binary
   218		representation: writing $\kappa$ for the binary representation with
   219		respect to the fixed self-dual normal basis
   220		(Definition~\ref{def:binary-representation}), item~2 of
   221		Lemma~\ref{lem:downsize_field} gives
   222		$\tr(c) = \tr(c \cdot 1) = \kappa(c) \cdot \kappa(1)$, and $\kappa(1)$
   223		is the all-ones vector by Lemma~\ref{lem:one}. As $\kappa$ is a
   224		bijection onto $\F_2^k$, a uniformly random element of $\F_q$ has trace
   225		$0$ with probability exactly $\frac12$. Combining, the probability that
   226		$\gamma(\omega) \neq 0$ is exactly $(1-q^{-1})^{m+1} \cdot \frac12$, and
   227		the probability that $\omega$ is commuting is the complement, which is
   228		at least $\frac12$.
   229	
   230		If $m \leq q$, then
   231		$(1-q^{-1})^{m+1} \geq (1-q^{-1})^{q+1} = (1-q^{-1})^{q} \cdot (1-q^{-1})$,
   232		a product of two positive functions of $q$ that are nondecreasing for
   233		$q \geq 2$, so it is minimized at $q = 2$, where it equals $2^{-3}$;
   234		hence the anticommuting probability is at least $2^{-4}$.
   235	
   236		Finally, suppose $m, d \geq 1$, and consider the first inequality of
   237		the display, which bounds the anticommuting probability from below.
   238		If $md > q$, that lower bound is negative --- it is the product of
   239		the positive factors $1 - q^{-m}$, $1 - q^{-1}$, and $\frac12$ with
   240		the negative factor $1 - md/q$ --- so the anticommuting probability,
   241		being nonnegative, exceeds it. If $md \leq q$, then by Bernoulli's
   242		inequality
   243		$(1-q^{-1})^{m} \geq 1 - m/q \geq 1 - md/q \geq (1-q^{-m})(1-md/q)$,
   244		where the last step multiplies the nonnegative quantity $1 - md/q$
   245		by $1 - q^{-m} \leq 1$; multiplying by $1 - q^{-1}$ shows that the
   246		anticommuting probability is at least the first displayed bound. For
   247		the second inequality of the display, expanding the product shows
   248		that $(1-q^{-m})(1-q^{-1})(1-md/q)$ exceeds
   249		$1 - q^{-m} - q^{-1} - md/q$ by
   250		$q^{-m-1} + \frac{md}{q} \big( q^{-m} + q^{-1} - q^{-m-1} \big)$,
   251		a sum of nonnegative terms whatever the sign of $1 - md/q$; since
   252		$md \geq 1$ gives $q^{-m} \leq q^{-1} \leq md/q$, the product is
   253		therefore at least $1 - 3md/q$.
   254		The commuting probability is at least
   255		$\frac12 \geq \big(1 - \frac{3md}{q}\big) \cdot \frac12$.
   256	\end{proof}

   258	\begin{remark}[Source correction: the anticommuting probability]
   259		\label{rem:omega-anticomm-prob-correction}
   260		In the source, the statement corresponding to
   261		Lemma~\ref{fact:omega-anticomm-prob} asserts only the two bounds of the
   262		final display, without the hypothesis $m, d \geq 1$, and its proof
   263		begins with the claims that $\mathrm{ind}_m(u_X)$ vanishes if and only
   264		if $u_X = 0$ and that $u_X = 0$ forces $\omega$ to be commuting. Both
   265		claims are incorrect: the coordinates of $\mathrm{ind}_m(u)$ sum to $1$
   266		for every $u \in \F_q^m$, so $\mathrm{ind}_m(u)$ never vanishes, and for
   267		$(q,m,d) = (2,1,0)$ the tuple $\omega = (0,0,1,1)$ is anticommuting.
   268		For $d = 0$ the bounds themselves fail: with $(q,m,d) = (2,1,0)$ ---
   269		a tuple with admissible field size and $m \mid q$, excluded from
   270		Definition~\ref{def:admissible} only by the requirement $d \geq 1$
   271		that the source leaves implicit --- the exact anticommuting
   272		probability
   273		$(1-q^{-1})^{m+1} \cdot \frac12 = \frac18$ is smaller than the claimed
   274		lower bound $\big(1 - \frac{3md}{q}\big) \cdot \frac12 = \frac12$. The
   275		proof given above therefore computes the probability exactly, using the
   276		characteristic-two product formula for
   277		$\mathrm{ind}_m(u_X) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_Z)$, in place of the
   278		source's argument via the Schwartz--Zippel lemma; the exact value also
   279		supplies the unconditional constant lower bounds used in the proof of
   280		Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-win-implications}.  The full comparison is in
   281		\cite{gap:qpbt_anticommuting-probability}.
   282	\end{remark}

   284	\begin{definition}[Closeness of question-indexed operators]
   285		\label{def:approx-question-indexed-operators}
   286		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.opDistSq}
   287		\leanok
   288		\uses{def:povm-distance}
   289		Let $\{A^x\}$ and $\{B^x\}$ be families of operators (not necessarily
   290		POVM elements) indexed by questions $x \in \mathcal{X}$ but not by
   291		answers, let $\mu$ be a distribution over $\mathcal{X}$, and let
   292		$\ket{\psi}$ be a state, both fixed by context. Write
   293		$A^x \approx_\delta B^x$ to denote
   294		\[
   295			\E_{x \sim \mu} \bra{\psi} (A^x - B^x)^\dagger (A^x - B^x) \ket{\psi} \,\leq\, O(\delta)\,.
   296		\]
   297		This extends the answer-indexed closeness of
   298		Definition~\ref{def:povm-distance} to answer-free families of operators,
   299		such as observables; as there, the right-hand side allows a hidden
   300		universal constant.

blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex-69-\begin{remark}[Choice of decoding map and the decoder--encoder identity]\label{rem:qld-decoding-identity}
blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:70:	The source states the constructions of this chapter in terms of its boolean decoding map (the case $H = \{0,1\}$ of Definition~\ref{def:decoding-map}) while describing that map as returning the string of \emph{all} evaluations of $g$ on the hypercube. The proofs require the latter reading, $H = \F_q$, which is adopted throughout this chapter: the linearity of $\mathrm{Dec}$ and the identity $\mathrm{Dec}(g_h) = h$ for all $h \in \F_q^{M}$, both of which fail for the boolean map, are used in the symmetry step of the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis}. The source further asserts the identity $\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u) = g(u)$ for every $g \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$. Since the left-hand side equals $g_{\mathrm{Dec}(g)}(u)$, the identity, taken for all $u \in \F_q^m$, states that the multilinear representative $g_{\mathrm{Dec}(g)}$ and $g$ induce the same function on $\F_q^m$. Every encoding satisfies it, because then $g_{\mathrm{Dec}(g)} = g$ as polynomial representatives; a polynomial that is not an encoding need not: for $m = 1$, $d \geq 2$, and $q > 2$, the polynomial $g(x) = x^2$ has $\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_1(u) = u$, which differs from $g(u) = u^2$ at every $u \notin \{0,1\}$. When $d \leq q-1$ the failure at some $u$ characterizes the polynomials that are not encodings, since evaluation is injective on representatives of individual degree at most $q-1$ (Definition~\ref{def:polynomials-degree}); when $d \geq q$ it does not: for the admissible tuple $(q,m,d) = (8,1,8)$, the polynomial $g(x) = x^8$ is not an encoding, yet $\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_1(u) = u = u^8 = g(u)$ for every $u \in \F_8$. Accordingly, the proofs below invoke the identity only for encodings; in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis} the contribution of the remaining outcomes is controlled by the bound \eqref{eq:qld-nonencoding-mass} on the mass that the measurement of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-7} places on polynomials that are not encodings, while in the conjugation identity \eqref{eq:qld-unitary-6} the quantity $\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u)$ cancels exactly.

blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex-73-\end{remark}

blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex-15-The classical low individual degree game is a two-player game based on the low individual degree variant of the multilinearity test of Babai, Fortnow, and Lund. In the basic version, one player (the ``points player'') receives a uniformly random point $u \in \F_q^m$ and answers with a value $a \in \F_q$, while the other player (the ``lines player'') receives a random line through $u$ --- either axis-parallel or diagonal --- and answers with a univariate polynomial describing the restriction of a global function to that line. If the players share a polynomial $g\colon \F_q^m \to \F_q$ of individual degree at most $d$ and answer with $g(u)$ and with the restriction $g|_\ell$, they win with probability $1$; the soundness theorem below states that the converse approximately holds. In the simultaneous version, the players' answers are $k$-tuples, checked coordinatewise against a $k$-tuple of low individual degree polynomials.

blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex-121-	The source states the two line-versus-point clauses with ``the'' $t \in \F_q$ such that $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v$. But zero directions occur: Definition~\ref{def:line} explicitly permits them, and the question distribution of Definition~\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} produces $\mathsf{DLine}$ questions with $v' = \pi_{i-1}(v) = 0$ with positive probability, namely whenever the last $m - i + 1$ coordinates of $v$ vanish. The universal quantification over $t$ adopted in Definition~\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} makes the predicate a well-defined function of its arguments; it accepts vacuously when no such $t$ exists, a case the question distribution never produces. Completeness is unaffected: the restriction of a polynomial $g$ to the singleton line $\ell(u_0,0)$, expressed through the parameterization $t \mapsto u_0 + t \cdot 0$, is the constant polynomial with value $g(u_0)$, which passes the check for every $t$. Soundness is likewise unaffected: zero directions occur with probability at most $2/(mq)$, so any acceptance convention on this event changes success probabilities by at most that amount; the game-correspondence obligation enumerated in the proof of Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness} accounts for this event explicitly, and an error of this shape is absorbed into the universal constants of $\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}$.

blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex-292-The Pauli basis test is the quantum low individual degree test of Natarajan and Vidick, in the slightly modified form introduced by Natarajan and Wright~\cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. Informally, the test certifies that the players share the state $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}$, where $M = 2^m$. On a question of type $(\mathsf{Pauli}, W)$ with $W \in \{X,Z\}$, a player is expected to measure the generalized Pauli basis POVM $\{\tau^W_h\}_{h \in \F_q^M}$ of Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra} and report the outcome $h$. Most subtests probe limited information about $h$: given a point $u_W \in \F_q^m$, a player is expected to report the evaluation $g_h(u_W)$ of the low-degree encoding $g_h$ of $h$, and for a fixed basis $W$ these probes are checked against each other by the classical low individual degree game of Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}. Consistency \emph{between} the two bases is checked through two-outcome probes: given additionally $r_W \in \F_q$, a player reports $\tr(g_h(u_W)\, r_W) \in \F_2$. The two binary measurements obtained in this way for $W = X$ and $W = Z$ either commute or anticommute, according to the value $\gamma \in \F_2$ of Equation~\eqref{eq:gamma-value} below. When $\gamma = 0$ the verifier checks commutation directly by asking for both bits simultaneously; when $\gamma = 1$ the verifier checks anticommutation by playing the Magic Square game, using Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}.

\section{Analysis of the Pauli basis test}
\label{sec:qld-analysis}
In this appendix we give a proof of \Cref{thm:pauli}. For
convenience, we repeat the statement of the theorem here.

\begin{theorem}
  \label{thm:pauli-appendix}
There exists a function 
\[\delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})\]
 for universal constants $a \geq 1$ and $0 < b < 1$ such that the following holds. For all admissible parameter tuples $\qldparams = (q,m,d)$ and for all strategies $\strategy = (\ket{\psi},A,B)$ for the game $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ that succeed with probability at least $1 - \eps$, there exist local isometries $\phi_\alice: \mH_\alice \to \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\alice''},\phi_\bob: \mH_\bob \to \mH_{\bob'} \otimes \mH_{\bob''}$ (where $\ket{\psi} \in \mH_\alice \otimes \mH_\bob$ and $\mH_{\alice''},\mH_{\bob''} \cong (\C^q)^{\otimes M}$ with $M = 2^m$) and a state $\ket{\aux} \in \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\bob'}$ such that 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\left \| \phi_\alice \otimes \phi_B \ket{\psi} - \ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}  \right \| \leq \delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q)$,
    \item Letting $\tilde{A}^x_a = \phi_A\, A^x_a \, \phi_A^\dagger$ and $\tilde{B}^y_b = \phi_B B^y_b \phi_B^\dagger$, we have for $W \in \{X,Z\}$
    \begin{gather*}
        \tilde{A}^{(\pauli,W)}_u \otimes I_{\bob'\bob''} \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} (\tau^W_u)_{\alice''} \otimes I_{\alice' \bob' \bob''} \\
        I_{\alice'\alice''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{(\pauli,W)}_u    \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} I_{\alice' \alice'' \bob'} \otimes (\tau^W_u)_{\bob''}\;,
    \end{gather*}
    where the $\approx_{\delta_{\qld}}$ statement holds with respect to the state $\ket{\aux}_{\alice'\bob'} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}_{\alice''\bob''}$ and the answer summation is over $u \in \F_q^M$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
We also recall the meaning of the parameters: $q$ is the field size,
$m$ the number of variables, $d$ the degree of the low-degree code,
and $\nqubits=2^m$ is the number of $\ket{\EPR_q}$ states being tested for.

This appendix is structured as follows. First, we establish some preliminary facts and definitions 
in \Cref{sec:qld-prelim}. In the remainder of the appendix, we
show \Cref{thm:pauli-appendix} by showing how to construct a representation of
the Pauli group on the provers' Hilbert space, starting from a
strategy $\strategy$ that succeeds in $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ with
high probability. This is done in several stages: in
\Cref{sec:commutation}, we use the strategy measurements to define a
set of observables that correspond to a subset of the Pauli $X$ and
$Z$ observables, and show that these
approximately satisfy the associated Pauli group relations. In \Cref{sec:expanding},
we adjoin ancillary registers containing EPR states to the provers'
state $\ket{\psi}$, and define a new set of approximately-commuting
observables acting on the expanded state. In \Cref{sec:combining}, we
combine the approximately-commuting observables into a strategy for
the \emph{classical} low-degree test, and in \Cref{sec:apply-ldt}, we
apply the soundness theorem of the classical low-degree test to
construct a single projective measurement that simultaneously measures all of the
approximately-commuting observables. Finally, in
\Cref{sec:separating}, we use this single simultaneous measurement to
construct an exact representation of the Pauli group, show that it
is close to the original strategy observables on the expanded state, and deduce that the game $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ is a self-test for the strategy $\strategy^\pauli$.

\subsection{Preliminaries}
\label{sec:qld-prelim}


\begin{definition}
Given integer $d,m$ and a prime power $q$ we denote by $\ideg_{d,m}(\F_q)$ the set of polynomials in $m$ variables
  with \emph{individual} degree at most $d$ in each variable. When the field is clear from context we write $\ideg_{d,m}$. 	
	When
  the number of variables is clear from context we
  write $\ideg_d$. We denote by $\deg_{d}$ the set of polynomials with
  \emph{total} degree at most $d$.
\end{definition}

Recall the low-degree code defined in \Cref{sec:ld-encoding}, in which vectors $h \in \F_q^\nqubits$ get mapped to polynomials $g_h \in \ideg_{d,m}(\F_q)$ such that for every $u \in \{0,1\}^m$, $g_h(u) = h_u$ where the coordinates of $h$ are indexed by binary strings of length $m$. For $x\in \F_q^m$, recall the definition of the vector $\ind_m(x) \in \F_q^\nqubits$ from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}. Recall also the finite field trace $\tr(\cdot)=\tr_{q\to 2}(\cdot):\F_q\to\F_2$, where $q=2^k$ for odd $k$, defined in Section~\ref{sec:subfields}. 



Call a tuple $\omega = (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,r_\xpt,r_\zpt) \in (\F_q^m)^2
\times (\F_q)^2$ \emph{anticommuting} if the quantity 
 \[\gamma\,=\,\tr ((r_\xpt \cdot
\ind_m(u_\xpt)) \cdot (r_\zpt \cdot \ind_m(u_\zpt)))\]
introduced in~\Cref{eq:gamma-value} is not $0$, and \emph{commuting} if $\gamma=0$.

\begin{fact}
\label{fact:omega-anticomm-prob}
	The probability that a tuple $\omega= (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)$ sampled uniformly at random from $(\F_q^m)^2 \times (\F_q)^2$
	is anti-commuting is at least 
	\[
		(1 - q^{-m}) \cdot (1 - q^{-1}) \cdot \Big (1 - \frac{md}{q} \Big )  \cdot \frac{1}{2} \geq \Big (1 - \frac{3md}{q} \Big ) \cdot \frac{1}{2}.

    59	representatives; `decodeFq` restricts its domain to the bounded-degree class
    60	`Poly P`. -/
    61	noncomputable abbrev decodeFq {P : AdmissibleParams} (g : Poly P) :
    62	    PauliRegister P :=
    63	  decodeOnUniv g
    64	
    65	/-! ## The encoding image -/
    66	
    67	/-- Membership of a multilinear encoding in the bounded representative class.
    68	
    69	Each indicator factor has degree zero away from its own variable and degree at
    70	most one in that variable, so the multilinear encoding has individual degree at
    71	most one, and hence at most `P.d` using `P.hd`.  This is the degree
    72	side-condition implicit in the source's `g_h` construction, not an extra
    73	hypothesis of the decoding identity.  See `def:low-degree-encoding`, blueprint
    74	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:404-424`, and paper
    75	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:832-897`. -/
    76	theorem lowDegreeEncoding_mem_poly {P : AdmissibleParams}
    77	    (h : PauliRegister P) :
    78	    lowDegreeEncoding h ∈
    79	      MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries.polyFunc P.m (PauliScalar P) P.d := by
    80	  rw [MvPolynomial.mem_restrictDegree]
    81	  intro s hs i
    82	  apply (MvPolynomial.monomial_le_degreeOf i hs).trans
    83	  rw [lowDegreeEncoding]
    84	  refine (MvPolynomial.degreeOf_sum_le i Finset.univ _).trans ?_
    85	  refine Finset.sup_le fun y _ => ?_
    86	  refine (show MvPolynomial.degreeOf i
    87	      (h y • indicatorPoly (K := PauliScalar P) y) ≤
    88	      MvPolynomial.degreeOf i (indicatorPoly (K := PauliScalar P) y) from ?_).trans ?_
    89	  · simpa only [MvPolynomial.smul_eq_C_mul] using
    90	      MvPolynomial.degreeOf_C_mul_le (indicatorPoly (K := PauliScalar P) y) i (h y)
    91	  rw [indicatorPoly]
    92	  refine (MvPolynomial.degreeOf_prod_le i Finset.univ _).trans ?_
    93	  calc
    94	    ∑ j, MvPolynomial.degreeOf i
    95	        (if y j then
    96	          (MvPolynomial.X j : MvPolynomial (Fin P.m) (PauliScalar P))
    97	        else 1 - MvPolynomial.X j) ≤
    98	        ∑ j, if i = j then 1 else 0 := by
    99	      apply Finset.sum_le_sum
   100	      intro j _
   101	      split
   102	      · exact le_of_eq (MvPolynomial.degreeOf_X i j)
   103	      · exact (MvPolynomial.degreeOf_sub_le i 1 (MvPolynomial.X j)).trans_eq (by
   104	          simp [MvPolynomial.degreeOf_X])
   105	    _ = 1 := by simp
   106	    _ ≤ P.d := P.hd
   107	
   108	/-- The multilinear encoding as a bounded polynomial representative.
   109	
   110	The individual-degree bound is supplied by `lowDegreeEncoding_mem_poly`. -/
   111	noncomputable def encodingPoly {P : AdmissibleParams} (h : PauliRegister P) :
   112	    Poly P :=
   113	  ⟨lowDegreeEncoding h, lowDegreeEncoding_mem_poly h⟩
   114	
   115	/-- A `Poly P` outcome is an encoding when its decoder reconstructs the same
   116	underlying polynomial representative.
   117	
   118	This is the explicit support restriction required by the corrected Chapter 16
   119	decoding argument.  It is the `Poly` view of `IsEncodingRep`; no unrestricted
   120	decoder/evaluation identity is asserted.  See
   121	`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_decoding-identity.tex:87-123`. -/
   122	def IsEncoding {P : AdmissibleParams} (g : Poly P) : Prop :=
   123	  lowDegreeEncoding (decodeFq g) = g.1
   124	
   125	/-! ## Decoder companions -/
   126	
   127	/-- Linearity of the full-field decoder on bounded representatives.
   128	
   129	This is the additive linearity of `lem:qld-decoder-linearity`, blueprint
   130	`ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:30-40`, used in the symmetry step of the source
   131	argument at
   132	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1546-1550`
   133	and blueprint `ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:239-244`.  It does not assert
   134	evaluation equality for non-encoding representatives.  See
   135	`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_decoding-identity.tex:87-123`. -/
   136	theorem decodeFq_add {P : AdmissibleParams} (g h : Poly P) :
   137	    decodeFq (g + h) = decodeFq g + decodeFq h := by
   138	  funext y
   139	  simp [decodeOn, decodeAt, evalPoly, MvPolynomial.eval_add]
   140	
   141	/-- Scalar linearity of the full-field decoder on bounded representatives.
   142	
   143	This companion has the same source scope as `decodeFq_add` and does not
   144	strengthen the restricted decoder identity.  See
   145	`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_decoding-identity.tex:87-123`. -/
   146	theorem decodeFq_smul {P : AdmissibleParams} (c : PauliScalar P) (g : Poly P) :
   147	    decodeFq (c • g) = c • decodeFq g := by
   148	  funext y
   149	  simp [decodeOn, decodeAt, evalPoly, MvPolynomial.smul_eval]
   150	
   151	/-- The full-field decoder is a left inverse to `encodingPoly`.
   152	
   153	This is the identity `\operatorname{Dec}(g_h)=h` of
   154	`lem:qld-decoder-linearity`, blueprint `ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:30-40`, for
   155	the full-field decoder specified at
   156	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1419-1420`.
   157	The degree proof is separated into `lowDegreeEncoding_mem_poly`; no additional
   158	encoding or interpolation hypothesis is introduced.  See
   159	`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_decoding-identity.tex:87-123`. -/
   160	theorem decodeFq_lowDegreeEncoding {P : AdmissibleParams}
   161	    (h : PauliRegister P) :
   162	    decodeFq (encodingPoly h) = h := by
   163	  funext y
   164	  simpa only [decodeFq, decodeOnUniv, decodeOn, decodeAt, evalPoly,
   165	    encodingPoly, lowDegreeEnc, Finset.mem_univ, if_true] using
   166	      congrFun
   167	        (decodeAt_lowDegreeEnc
   168	          (Finset.univ : Finset (PauliScalar P)) h
   169	            (fun z => Finset.mem_univ (h z))) y
   170	
   171	/-- Decoder/evaluation agreement for an encoding representative only.
   172	
   173	The hypothesis `hg : IsEncoding g` is mandatory.  For a general bounded
   174	polynomial, Boolean-cube values determine its multilinear interpolant, which
   175	need not equal the original representative.  This is the corrected form of
   176	the source step at
   177	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1483-1492`;
   178	see `docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_decoding-identity.tex:87-123`.
   179	
   180	**Local fix:** The source's unrestricted identity is false, as witnessed by
   181	`g(x) = x^2` over a field with more than two elements.  The encoding restriction
   182	and representative semantics are documented in
   183	`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_decoding-identity.tex:87-123`. -/
   184	theorem decodeFq_dotProduct_indicatorVec {P : AdmissibleParams}
   185	    {g : Poly P} (hg : IsEncoding g) (x : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) :
   186	    dotProduct (decodeFq g) (indicatorVec x) = evalPoly g x := by
   187	  unfold IsEncoding at hg
   188	  calc
   189	    dotProduct (decodeFq g) (indicatorVec x) = lowDegreeEnc (decodeFq g) x :=
   190	      (lowDegreeEnc_eq_dotProduct (decodeFq g) x).symm
   191	    _ = evalPoly g x := by simp [lowDegreeEnc, evalPoly, hg]
   192	
   193	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

    12	\title{The Decoding Identity in the Pauli Extraction Argument}
    13	\author{}
    14	\date{2026-09-03}
    15	
    16	\begin{document}
    17	\maketitle
    18	
    19	\section{At a glance}
    20	
    21	\begin{itemize}
    22	  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Medium.  The source applies a decoder--encoder
    23	  identity to every bounded individual-degree polynomial, although the identity
    24	  is guaranteed for encoded polynomials and can fail outside the encoding image.
    25	  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} One restricted algebraic identity and one
    26	  probabilistic estimate showing that the constructed measurement assigns
    27	  little state-dependent mass to outcomes outside the encoding image.
    28	  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} Evaluation of the multilinear
    29	  interpolant is elementary polynomial algebra.  The non-encoding-mass bound
    30	  uses project-specific consistency estimates and Schwartz--Zippel.
    31	  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} Multilinear interpolation on the
    32	  Boolean cube, injectivity of the low-degree encoding, measurement
    33	  consistency, and Schwartz--Zippel.  The correction is tracked in
    34	  \ghissue{19}.
    35	\end{itemize}
    36	
    37	\section{Key theorem forms}
    38	
    39	For a word $h\colon\{0,1\}^m\to\mathbb F_q$, let $g_h$ be its multilinear
    40	extension.  Define the chapter's decoder by
    41	\[
    42	  \operatorname{Dec}(g)(y)=g(y),
    43	  \qquad y\in\{0,1\}^m.
    44	\]
    45	Then
    46	\[
    47	  \operatorname{Dec}(g_h)=h
    48	  \quad\text{and}\quad
    49	  \operatorname{Dec}(g_h)\mathbin{\cdot}\operatorname{ind}_m(u)=g_h(u).
    50	\]
    51	More generally, the second identity holds for a polynomial outcome $g$ under
    52	the explicit hypothesis that $g$ belongs to the image of the encoding; no
    53	converse is asserted.
    54	
    55	For an arbitrary bounded individual-degree polynomial $g$, the Boolean values
    56	determine its multilinear interpolant, not necessarily $g$ itself.  The
    57	unrestricted identity
    58	\[
    59	  \operatorname{Dec}(g)\mathbin{\cdot}\operatorname{ind}_m(u)=g(u)
    60	\]
    61	is therefore false.
    62	
    63	\section{Counterexample and source comparison}
    64	
    65	The low-degree encoding is defined at lines~873--897 of
    66	\path{references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex}.  The general decoder at
    67	lines~917--924 retains evaluations lying in a chosen subset $H$; the extraction
    68	chapter instead specifies at lines~1419--1420 of
    69	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex} that the
    70	decoder returns all evaluations on the Boolean cube.  This is the specialization
    71	$H=\mathbb F_q$, rather than the Boolean-valued shorthand used earlier
    72	\cite[lines~873--924 and 1419--1420]{Ji2020MIPStar}.
    73	
    74	Take $m=1$, $d\geq2$, and a field of characteristic two with more than two
    75	elements.  For $g(x)=x^2$, the Boolean evaluations are $g(0)=0$ and $g(1)=1$.
    76	Consequently the decoder is the word whose multilinear extension is $x$.
    77	For any $u\notin\{0,1\}$ with $u^2\neq u$,
    78	\[
    79	  \operatorname{Dec}(g)\mathbin{\cdot}\operatorname{ind}_1(u)=u
    80	  \neq u^2=g(u).
    81	\]
    82	Thus the equality asserted for every $g$ at lines~1483--1492 of the chapter-14
    83	source mirror is false \cite[lines~1483--1492]{Ji2020MIPStar}.  If degrees at
    84	least $q$ are allowed, equality as a function would not by itself prove encoding
    85	membership either, since $x^q$ and $x$ induce the same function on $\mathbb F_q$.
    86	
    87	\section{Required repair}
    88	
    89	The extraction proof must split the marginal measurement into encoding and
    90	non-encoding outcomes.  On encoding outcomes, the restricted identity above
    91	justifies the substitution.  On the complement, the proof must bound
    92	\[
    93	  \sum_{g\ \mathrm{not\ an\ encoding}}
    94	  \langle\widehat\psi,\widehat S_g^W\widehat\psi\rangle.
    95	\]
    96	The blueprint derives an $O(\delta_S)+md/q$ bound from point consistency and
    97	the combined point measurement.  A non-encoding polynomial differs from every
    98	encoded polynomial, so Schwartz--Zippel bounds the probability that their
    99	evaluations coincide.  This estimate is the open reduction; it must be proved
   100	from the paper hypotheses rather than inserted as an extraction hypothesis.
   101	
   102	The printed reindexing at lines~1805--1822 replaces
   103	$g_{\operatorname{Dec}(g_W)}$ by $g_W$, which is the invalid reverse identity
   104	for an arbitrary polynomial outcome.  In the corrected calculation, the
   105	constraint is
   106	$g_h(u)=\operatorname{Dec}(g_W)\mathbin{\cdot}\operatorname{ind}_m(u)-a$.
   107	After setting $h'=h+\operatorname{Dec}(g_W)$, the defining evaluation formula
   108	$g_k(u)=k\mathbin{\cdot}\operatorname{ind}_m(u)$ and characteristic two turn
   109	that constraint into $g_{h'}(u)=a$.  Thus this step uses neither decoder
   110	linearity nor the identity $\operatorname{Dec}(g_h)=h$
   111	\cite[lines~1805--1822]{Ji2020MIPStar}.
   112	
   113	\section{Blueprint and formalization status}
   114	
   115	Definition~\path{def:qld-full-field-decoder} and
   116	Lemmas~\path{lem:qld-decoder-linearity} and
   117	\path{lem:qld-decoder-evaluation} in
   118	\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex} state the full-field
   119	decoder, its linearity and inverse, and the evaluation identity restricted to
   120	encoding outcomes.  Lemma~\path{lem:qld-nonencoding-mass-bound}
   121	separately records the estimate on the remaining outcomes.
   122	
   123	The declarations \path{decodeFq_add}, \path{decodeFq_smul}, and
   124	\path{decodeFq_lowDegreeEncoding} in
   125	\path{MIPStarRE/QPBT/Algebra/Decoding.lean} match the three algebraic assertions.
   126	In the same file, \path{IsEncoding} is the equality
   127	$g_{\operatorname{Dec}(g)}=g$ of polynomial representatives, and
   128	\path{decodeFq_dotProduct_indicatorVec} requires an explicit hypothesis
   129	of that predicate.  It therefore matches the corrected evaluation lemma and
   130	does not assert the false unrestricted identity.  Finally,
   131	\path{nonencodingMarginalMass_le} in
   132	\path{MIPStarRE/QPBT/Extraction/Consistency.lean} concludes the complementary
   133	mass bound from the projective strategy and global polynomial-pair witness; it
   134	does not add the bound as a witness field or theorem hypothesis.
   135	
   136	The decoder calculations are proved.  \path{lowDegreeEncoding_mem_poly},
   137	\path{decodeFq_add}, \path{decodeFq_smul}, \path{decodeFq_lowDegreeEncoding},
   138	and \path{decodeFq_dotProduct_indicatorVec} carry complete proofs: the degree
   139	side-condition on $g_h$, the two linearity laws, the inversion
   140	$\operatorname{Dec}_{\mathbb F_q}(g_h)=h$, and the evaluation identity under the
   141	explicit \path{IsEncoding} hypothesis.  The complementary estimate
   142	\path{nonencodingMarginalMass_le} is the remaining open proof of this note.
   143	Issue~\#19 owns the Stage~4.2 statements and this discrepancy record;
   144	\ghissue{47} owns the Stage~4.3 decoder calculations, now discharged, and the
   145	non-encoding support estimate.  No unrestricted theorem, residual assumption, or
   146	additional witness field was introduced.
   147	
   148	\section{Conclusion}
   149	
   150	The decoding identity is false for a general polynomial outcome.  Restricting
   151	it to the encoding image is a necessary local correction.  Recovering the
   152	source's measurement-consistency conclusion then requires the separate
   153	non-encoding-mass estimate, which remains an open proof obligation.
   154

    12	\title{Triangle Estimates and Isometry Transfer in Pauli Extraction}
    13	\author{}
    14	\date{2026-09-03}
    15	
    16	\begin{document}
    17	\maketitle
    18	
    19	\section{At a glance}
    20	
    21	\begin{itemize}
    22	  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Medium.  The extraction proof contains two
    23	  incorrect numerical steps and later suppresses the range projection when
    24	  passing from unitary conjugation to isometry conjugation.
    25	  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} A corrected positive-contraction estimate,
    26	  a small-error case split for normalization, and one range-projection transfer
    27	  lemma for a projective measurement family.
    28	  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} Positivity, contraction inequalities,
    29	  isometry range projections, and norm estimates belong to finite-dimensional
    30	  Hilbert-space algebra.  The state-dependent family distance and register
    31	  placements are project-local.
    32	  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} The inequality
    33	  $H^2\geq2H-I$ for a positive contraction, the triangle inequality, and
    34	  $Q=\phi\phi^\dagger$ for an isometry.  The repair is tracked in
    35	  \ghissue{19}.
    36	\end{itemize}
    37	
    38	\section{Key theorem forms}
    39	
    40	Let $H_X$ and $H_Z$ be the positive contractions of the extraction proof, and
    41	let $\vartheta$ be a unit vector such that
    42	\[
    43	  \langle\vartheta,H_W\vartheta\rangle\geq1-\delta/2
    44	  \qquad (W\in\{X,Z\}).
    45	\]
    46	Since $(I-H_W)^2\geq0$,
    47	\[
    48	  H_W^2\geq2H_W-I,
    49	  \qquad
    50	  \langle\vartheta,H_W^2\vartheta\rangle\geq1-\delta.
    51	\]
    52	Also $\lVert(I-H_W)\vartheta\rVert^2\leq\delta$, whence
    53	\[
    54	  \lVert H_X\vartheta-H_Z\vartheta\rVert^2\leq4\delta.
    55	\]
    56	Together with $H_XH_Z$ equal to the EPR projection, these estimates give the
    57	required overlap bound, with constants absorbed into the stated
    58	$O(\sqrt\delta)$ error.
    59	
    60	For the final transfer, let $\phi\colon\mathcal H\to\mathcal K$ be an isometry
    61	and set $Q=\phi\phi^\dagger$.  If $N_h$ is the unitary-conjugated extension of
    62	a measurement operator $M_h$, then the exact identity is
    63	\[
    64	  \phi M_h\phi^\dagger=N_hQ=QN_h,
    65	\]
    66	not merely $N_h$.  Thus comparison of $N_h$ with an ideal projector must be
    67	combined with control of $(I-Q)\Delta$ on the ideal comparison state
    68	$\Delta$.
    69	
    70	\section{Numerical defects in the source proof}
    71	
    72	Lines~1715--1742 of
    73	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex}
    74	construct $H_X,H_Z$ and identify $H_XH_Z$ with the EPR projection.  The norm
    75	estimate at lines~1743--1750 gives
    76	$\lVert(I-H_W)\vartheta\rVert\leq\sqrt\delta$.  At lines~1753--1757 the
    77	source substitutes $\delta$ inside the reverse triangle inequality
    78	\cite[lines~1715--1783]{Ji2020MIPStar}.  That replacement is not valid for
    79	small $\delta$.  The desired lower bound on
    80	$\langle H_W^2\rangle$ follows directly from $H_W^2\geq2H_W-I$, as above.
    81	
    82	The triangle inequality yields
    83	\[
    84	  \lVert H_X\vartheta-H_Z\vartheta\rVert\leq2\sqrt\delta,
    85	\]
    86	so its square is at most $4\delta$.  Line~1761 instead bounds that square by
    87	$2\sqrt\delta$ without a stated restriction.  This inequality follows when
    88	$\delta\leq1/4$; for larger error the theorem is made trivial by enlarging the
    89	universal constant.  The same small-error split ensures that the projected
    90	vector defined at lines~1769--1773 is nonzero before it is normalized.  These
    91	are local numerical repairs and do not weaken the extraction conclusion.
    92	
    93	\section{The range-projection obligation}
    94	
    95	Lines~1827--1858 prove state-dependent closeness for the concrete operators
    96	obtained by conjugating the original measurement with the swap unitaries.
    97	Lines~1864--1875 then define isometries by adjoining EPR pairs and applying
    98	those unitaries, and immediately state the corresponding closeness for
    99	$\phi M_h\phi^\dagger$.  The omitted range projection makes this implication
   100	non-definitional \cite[lines~1827--1875]{Ji2020MIPStar}.
   101	
   102	Let $\Psi$ be the original state and suppose $\phi\Psi$ is close to the ideal
   103	state $\Delta$.  Since $Q\phi\Psi=\phi\Psi$ and $Q$ is a contraction, the
   104	triangle inequality bounds $(I-Q)\Delta$ by the state-extraction error.  Using
   105	$\phi M_h\phi^\dagger=N_hQ$, split
   106	\[
   107	  (N_hQ-T_h)\Delta
   108	  =(N_h-T_h)\Delta-N_h(I-Q)\Delta,
   109	\]
   110	where $T_h$ is the ideal Pauli projector.  Summing squared norms over $h$

    58	\paragraph{Proof obligation.}
    59	A proof obligation is an intermediate assertion needed by the proof of a source
    60	theorem.  It may be a construction, an estimate, a transport lemma, or a
    61	comparison between two formal representations.  If the paper proves or invokes
    62	this assertion, then the formalization should state it as a separate lemma or
    63	theorem and prove it from the upstream hypotheses.
    64	
    65	\paragraph{Obligation discharger.}
    66	An obligation discharger is a theorem or definition which constructs a proof
    67	obligation from the paper hypotheses already available at that point in the
    68	argument.  This is the preferred representation of missing work.  If the proof
    69	is not yet complete, the discharger may temporarily contain a tracked
    70	\verb|sorry|, but the paper-facing theorem should call it rather than assume
    71	its output as an additional theorem hypothesis.
    72	
    73	\paragraph{Conditional helper.}
    74	A conditional helper is a separately named theorem whose statement explicitly
    75	assumes a proof obligation.  Names such as
    76	\leanid{mainFormal\_ofInternalObligations},
    77	\leanid{orthonormalization\_ofInput}, or names whose suffix advertises the
    78	assumed obligation are permitted only when the declaration is not presented as
    79	the source theorem.  A conditional helper is a quarantine for downstream proof
    80	content; it does not close the source theorem.
    81	
    82	\section{Bridge, residual, repair, input, and obligation structures}
    83	
    84	The words \emph{bridge}, \emph{residual}, \emph{repair}, \emph{input}, and
    85	\emph{obligation structure} name possible formal shapes.  They become dangerous
    86	when their mathematical status is unclear or when their names make unproved
    87	data look like acceptable hypotheses of a source theorem.
    88	
    89	\paragraph{Bridge.}
    90	A bridge should be a transport theorem between two already defined
    91	mathematical forms: for example, a tensor-placement identity, a conversion
    92	between two equivalent consistency relations, or a statement translating a
    93	source object into a formal representation.  A bridge is harmless only after it
    94	is proved from previously available assumptions.  It becomes proof debt when it
    95	is assumed because the transport has not yet been proved.  It becomes theorem
    96	drift when the assumed bridge is added to a paper-facing theorem.
    97	
    98	\paragraph{Residual.}
    99	A residual is a named remainder after part of an argument has been performed.
   100	It is often a useful way to record the exact missing target after a completed
   101	construction.  A residual may appear as the conclusion of a helper theorem or
   102	as the input of a quarantined conditional helper.  It is not a permissible new
   103	assumption on a paper theorem unless the paper itself assumes that residual.
   104	
   105	\paragraph{Input.}
   106	An input is a named bundle of data or hypotheses consumed by a construction or
   107	conditional helper.  It is harmless only when each load-bearing field is either
   108	part of the source hypotheses or is produced by an earlier theorem.  It becomes
   109	proof debt when the bundle is merely assumed because the construction of its
   110	fields is missing.  It becomes theorem drift when such a bundle is added to the
   111	public statement of a source theorem.
   112	
   113	\paragraph{Repair.}
   114	A repair is a mathematical construction which replaces an approximate or
   115	partial object by a better object, usually with a quantitative estimate.  In
   116	the low individual degree test formalization, projectivization and
   117	orthonormalization repairs are genuine mathematical operations.  A repair
   118	should therefore appear as a construction or as a theorem discharging the
   119	corresponding obligation.  If a theorem assumes the output of the repair instead
   120	of constructing it, that theorem is conditional on the repair.
   121	
   122	\paragraph{Obligation structure.}
   123	An obligation structure is a record whose fields are the data and estimates
   124	needed by a later construction.  This is acceptable only as an internal target
   125	or as a hypothesis of a conditional helper.  Such a structure becomes statement
   126	drift if it is added to a paper-facing theorem instead of being constructed
   127	inside the proof.  The review question is whether every load-bearing field is
   128	proved from the source hypotheses or is explicitly tracked as a missing
   129	obligation.
   130	
   131	\section{The main failure mode}
   132	
   133	Suppose the paper proves
   134	\[
   135	  H \Longrightarrow C.
   136	\]
   137	During formalization, the proof may need an intermediate assertion \(B\).  The
   138	paper theorem should be represented as
   139	\[
   140	  H \Longrightarrow B \Longrightarrow C
   141	  \quad\text{inside the proof,}
   142	\]
   143	where \(B\) is obtained by a lemma or theorem from \(H\).  The following
   144	public statement is a different theorem:
   145	\[
   146	  H \land B \Longrightarrow C.
   147	\]
   148	It is not unsound in \Lean{}, but it is not the paper theorem.  It says that the
   149	conclusion follows if the missing bridge data is supplied.  Such a theorem is a
   150	conditional helper, even if its conclusion looks exactly like the paper's
   151	conclusion.
   152	
   153	This is the situation colloquially described as ``adding a bridge
   154	hypothesis''.  More precisely, an unproved intermediate step has been promoted
   155	from the proof body to the theorem's assumptions.  The correction is not to hide
   156	the hypothesis under a different structure name.  The correction is to keep a
   157	paper-facing theorem with the source statement and move the missing step to a
   158	named internal proof obligation.
   159	
   160	\section{Faithful boundary hypotheses}
   161	
   162	Not every extra formal hypothesis is a theorem drift.  Some hypotheses are
   163	faithful boundary conditions introduced by formal encoding.  Examples include
   164	nonnegativity needed for a real power, positivity needed to divide by a
   165	quantity, finiteness and nonemptiness of an index type, a field-model instance,
   166	or decidability instances required by \Lean{}.  Such hypotheses are acceptable
   167	when they express part of the mathematical ambient setting or make explicit a
   168	condition used implicitly in the paper.
   169	
   170	The distinction is load-bearing.  A faithful boundary hypothesis describes the
   171	domain in which the paper's objects live.  A proof-debt hypothesis supplies a
   172	mathematical step that the proof should derive.  If removing the hypothesis
   173	leaves an unproved construction or estimate from the paper proof, then the
   174	hypothesis is proof debt, not a boundary condition.
   175	
   176	\section{Definition drift and subtree repair}
   177	
   178	Definition drift is especially dangerous because it propagates.  If a
   179	definition is changed so that it no longer denotes the object in the paper,
   180	then every downstream theorem using that definition may continue to compile

   231	When a source-labelled proof is blocked, use the following order.
   232	
   233	\begin{enumerate}
   234	  \item Read the cited source statement and the proof passage in
   235	  \path{references/ldt-paper/}.
   236	  \item Write the paper theorem form, the current \Lean{} theorem form, and the
   237	  first missing intermediate assertion.
   238	  \item Decide whether the missing assertion is a faithful boundary condition,
   239	  a representation adapter, an ordinary lemma from the paper proof, or a real
   240	  paper-gap discrepancy.
   241	  \item If it is an ordinary lemma or adapter, create a named theorem which
   242	  discharges that obligation.  Do not add it to the source theorem as a new
   243	  hypothesis.
   244	  \item Keep the source-labelled theorem itself in the source form, even if its
   245	  proof must contain a tracked \verb|sorry|.  This is the default repair when
   246	  the missing assertion has not yet been proved.
   247	  \item Create a conditional helper only to quarantine substantial proof content
   248	  that already exists and would otherwise be lost.  Do not create such a helper
   249	  merely to avoid a \verb|sorry| or to keep making progress.  If a conditional
   250	  helper remains, give it a conditional name, keep it separate from the
   251	  paper-facing theorem, and record the obligation discharger that must eliminate
   252	  it.
   253	  \item If the source and formal statements genuinely differ, write or update a
   254	  note under \path{docs/paper-gaps/} before marking the statement as aligned.
   255	  \item Update the blueprint so that paper labels point only to paper-facing
   256	  declarations.  Conditional helpers belong in remarks or implementation
   257	  notes, not in the source theorem block.
   258	\end{enumerate}
   259	
   260	\section{Retirement criterion}
   261	
   262	An auxiliary declaration should be removed from the main blueprint route, or
   263	renamed and documented as a purely internal lemma, when all three of the
   264	following conditions hold:
   265	\begin{enumerate}
   266	  \item it is not a statement in the cited paper and is not an explicitly cited
   267	        outside result;
   268	  \item no current proof of a paper-level target needs it as stated;
   269	  \item it assumes stronger proof data, finite-length data, completion data,
   270	        repair data, synchronization data, or package fields than the paper
   271	        proof requires.
   272	\end{enumerate}
   273	If such a declaration is still useful as a formal intermediate result, it
   274	should remain a lemma or a visibly conditional helper with a planned discharge.
   275	It should not be a headline replacement for the paper theorem, and it should
   276	not support a source-labelled blueprint \verb|\leanok| claim.
   277	
   278	\section{Review questions}
   279	
   280	A reviewer should first compare every paper-labelled declaration with the cited
   281	source statement, checking both hypotheses and conclusion up to faithful formal
   282	encoding.  Bridge, residual, repair, input, obligation-structure, and
   283	proof-obligation assumptions should be absent from paper-facing theorem
   284	signatures unless they occur in the paper.  If a conditional helper remains,
   285	its name should be explicitly conditional and it should not support a source
   286	theorem \verb|\leanok| claim.
   287	Each load-bearing obligation-structure or input field should have a theorem
   288	discharging it, a tracked issue, or an explicit \verb|sorry| at the obligation
   289	site.  When a definition has changed, the downstream subtree should be checked
   290	against the corrected definition rather than patched locally.  Finally, if the
   291	formal statement genuinely differs from the source statement, a paper-gap note
   292	should explain the mathematical difference and give a plan to remove or justify
   293	it.
   294	
   295	\section{Conclusion}
   296	
   297	The project should prefer visible proof obligations over invisible statement
   298	drift.  A tracked \verb|sorry| in the source-shaped theorem, or in the lowest
   299	named internal obligation needed by its proof, is less misleading than a source
   300	theorem whose assumptions have been strengthened.  Conditional helpers are not a
   301	normal substitute for unfinished proofs; they are temporary quarantines for
   302	substantial proof content, and they must remain conditional until the missing
   303	obligation is discharged.  The paper-facing declaration is reserved for the
   304	theorem proved by the paper, or for a documented corrected version whose
   305	mathematical difference is explicit.

    42	\section{Key theorem forms}
    43	
    44	Let $S$ and $T$ be binary observables and let $\rho$ be a positive
    45	semidefinite operator of trace one.  We distinguish the state-dependent
    46	operator distance from the distance between their associated binary projective
    47	measurements:
    48	\begin{align*}
    49	  d_\rho(S,T)^2
    50	    &:= \Re\tr\big((S-T)^\dagger(S-T)\rho\big), \\
    51	  \dbin_\rho(S,T)^2
    52	    &:= \sum_{s\in\{+,-\}}
    53	      \Re\tr\big((P_S^s-P_T^s)^\dagger
    54	                       (P_S^s-P_T^s)\rho\big),
    55	  \qquad P_S^\pm := \frac{\Id\pm S}{2}.
    56	\end{align*}
    57	The normalization and correlation identities are
    58	\begin{align}
    59	  \dbin_\rho(S,T)^2 &= \frac12 d_\rho(S,T)^2,
    60	    \tag{normalization}\label{eq:normalization}\\
    61	  d_\rho(S,T)^2
    62	    &= 2-2\Re\tr(ST\rho),
    63	    \tag{operator correlation}\label{eq:operator-correlation}\\
    64	  \dbin_\rho(S,T)^2
    65	    &= 1-\Re\tr(ST\rho).
    66	    \tag{binary correlation}\label{eq:binary-correlation}
    67	\end{align}
    68	Consequently, the conclusion delivered by the quantum linearity argument can
    69	be written either as
    70	\[
    71	  \mathbb E_a\dbin_{\rho'}(\mathcal A(a),A(a))^2\leq\delta
    72	\]
    73	or, equivalently, as
    74	\[
    75	  \mathbb E_a d_{\rho'}(\mathcal A(a),A(a))^2\leq2\delta.
    76	\]
    77	These are not equivalent to the same bound $\delta$ for the mean squared
    78	state-dependent operator distance.%
    79	\footnote{The formal declarations are \leanid{binaryObservableEffect},
    80	\leanid{binaryObservableDistSq},
    81	\leanid{binaryObservableDistSq\_eq\_stateDepDistSq\_div\_two},
    82	\leanid{stateDepDistSq\_eq\_two\_sub\_two\_mul\_correlation}, and
    83	\leanid{binaryObservableDistSq\_eq\_one\_sub\_correlation} in
    84	\doclink{MIPStarRE/QPBT/Combining/Linearity/BooleanFourier.lean}.}
    85	
    86	\section{The source calculation}
    87	
    88	Natarajan and Vidick define the distance between two POVMs by summing the
    89	squared state-dependent distances between corresponding square roots
    90	\cite[Section~3.1]{Natarajan2017Linearity}.  For projective measurements the
    91	square roots are the effects themselves.  In the binary case their calculation
    92	expands $P_S^\pm=(\Id\pm S)/2$ and obtains
    93	\[
    94	  \dbin_\rho(S,T)^2
    95	    = 1-\frac12\tr_\rho(ST+TS)
    96	    = \frac12\tr_\rho((S-T)^2).
    97	  \tag{source equation (3)}
    98	\]
    99	This is equation~(3) at lines~903--910 of the in-repository source mirror.%
   100	\footnote{See
   101	\path{references/nv-paper/fullpaper.tex}, lines~866--912.  The quantum
   102	linearity theorem and its Fourier--Naimark proof are at lines~1074--1112.}
   103	The next line identifies the final expression with the squared state-dependent
   104	operator distance.  The operator-distance definition at lines~873--875 is
   105	printed with $\rho$ occurring twice,
   106	\[
   107	  d_\rho(S,T)^2 = \tr_\rho\big((S-T)^\dagger(S-T)\rho\big),
   108	  \qquad \tr_\rho(X) := \tr(\rho X),
   109	\]
   110	and we read the duplication as typographical, keeping the single $\rho$ of the
   111	definition of $d$ above.  Under that reading the squared state-dependent
   112	operator distance is $\tr_\rho((S-T)^2)$ rather than one half of that
   113	quantity.  Thus the calculation through line~910 is correct and the equality
   114	on line~911 loses a factor of two.
   115	
   116	The Fourier--Naimark proof is consistent with the measurement normalization.
   117	It proves
   118	\[
   119	  \mathbb E_a\operatorname{CON}_{\rho'}(A(a),\mathcal A(a))
   120	  = \frac12+\frac12\mathbb E_{a,b}
   121	       \tr_\rho(A(a)A(b)A(a+b)).
   122	\]
   123	The hypothesis therefore makes the consistency deficit at most $\delta/2$.
   124	For binary projective measurements, the squared measurement distance is twice
   125	that deficit, giving the bound $\delta$ for the squared binary-measurement
   126	distance and the bound $2\delta$ for the squared state-dependent operator
   127	distance.
   128	
   129	\section{A four-point counterexample}
   130	
   131	The bound $\delta$ for the mean squared state-dependent operator distance is
   132	false.  Let $G=(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^2$, choose $r\in G\setminus\{0\}$, take
   133	the one-dimensional state $\rho=1$, and define scalar binary observables by
   134	\[
   135	  A(a)=\begin{cases}
   136	    -1,&a=r,\\
   137	     1,&a\neq r.
   138	  \end{cases}
   139	\]
   140	For the characters $\chi_u(a)=(-1)^{u\cdot a}$, the normalized Fourier
   141	coefficients satisfy
   142	\[
   143	  \widehat A(0)=\frac12,
   144	  \qquad
   145	  \widehat A(u)=-\frac12\chi_u(r)\quad(u\neq0).
   146	\]
   147	Their multiset is
   148	$\{\frac12,\frac12,\frac12,-\frac12\}$, and hence
   149	\[
   150	  \mathbb E_{a,b}A(a)A(b)A(a+b)
   151	    =\sum_u\widehat A(u)^3=\frac14.
   152	\]
   153	The correlation hypothesis therefore holds with $\delta=3/4$.
   154	
   155	Every scalar exact Boolean representation is one of the characters $\chi_u$,
   156	and its mean squared state-dependent operator distance from $A$ is
   157	\[
   158	  \mathbb E_a |A(a)-\chi_u(a)|^2
   159	    =2-2\widehat A(u)\geq1.
   160	\]
   161	Allowing an ancillary space does not reduce this lower bound.  Exact linearity
   162	and the binary-observable relations make the operators $\mathcal A(a)$ a
   163	commuting family of Hermitian involutions.  Their simultaneous spectral
   164	subspaces carry characters of $G$.  Evaluation in any density operator is
   165	therefore a convex combination of the scalar character correlations above, so
   166	the mean squared state-dependent operator distance remains at least $1$.  It
   167	cannot be at most $\delta=3/4$.  By~\eqref{eq:normalization}, the corresponding
   168	mean squared binary-measurement distance has lower bound $1/2$, which is
   169	compatible with the provider's conclusion.

    19	\section{At a glance}
    20	
    21	\begin{itemize}
    22	  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Medium.  The source quotes a fiberwise consequence
    23	  of a state-dependent quantum linearity theorem, but suppresses two averages,
    24	  loses a factor of two when converting measurement distance to operator
    25	  distance, and leaves implicit a compatibility argument for the auxiliary
    26	  spaces.

    35	  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} Theorem~10 of

    41	\section{Key theorem forms}
    42	
    43	Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, let $\rho$ be an arbitrary
    44	density operator on $H$, and let $u\mapsto O^u$ be binary observables on $H$,
    45	indexed by $\mathbb F_2^t$.  The cited theorem assumes the averaged
    46	correlation estimate
    47	\[
    48	  \mathop{\mathbb E}_{u,v}
    49	  \operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(
    50	    O^u O^v O^{u+v}\rho\right) \geq 1-\delta.
    51	\]
    52	Its Fourier--Naimark argument produces an auxiliary space $H'$, a unit vector
    53	$\mathrm{anc}\in H'$, and binary observables $L^u$ on $H\otimes H'$ satisfying,
    54	with
    55	$\rho'=\rho\otimes|\mathrm{anc}\rangle\langle\mathrm{anc}|$,
    56	\[
    57	  L^uL^v=L^{u+v}
    58	  \quad\text{for every }u,v.
    59	\]
    60	Moreover,
    61	\[
    62	  \mathop{\mathbb E}_{u}
    63	  \operatorname{Tr}\!\left((L^u-O^u\otimes I_{H'})^\dagger
    64	    (L^u-O^u\otimes I_{H'})\,\rho'\right)\leq2\delta.
    65	\]
    66	Equivalently, if $d^{\mathrm{bin}}_{\rho'}$ denotes the distance between the
    67	binary projective measurements associated with the two observables, then
    68	\[
    69	  \mathop{\mathbb E}_{u}
    70	  d^{\mathrm{bin}}_{\rho'}(L^u,O^u\otimes I_{H'})^2\leq\delta.
    71	\]
    72	The source prints $\delta$ for the first, operator-distance bound.  Its
    73	calculation instead proves the second, measurement-distance bound, which is
    74	one half of the squared operator distance.  The factor-of-two discrepancy and
    75	a counterexample to the printed operator bound are given in
    76	\path{docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_linearity-distance-normalization.tex}, tracked in
    77	\ghissue{124}.
    78	In particular, $L^0=I$: exact linearity gives $(L^0)^2=L^0$, while an
    79	observable is invertible.
    80	
    81	The chapter needs a parameterized version.  For each pair $(x,z)$ it applies
    82	the theorem to $(r,s)\mapsto O^{x,z,r,s}$.  If $\delta_{x,z}$ is the mean
    83	squared multiplicative defect on that fiber, the corresponding correlation
    84	error is $\delta_{x,z}/2$.  The corrected theorem therefore gives mean squared
    85	operator distance at most $\delta_{x,z}$, equivalently mean squared binary-
    86	measurement distance at most $\delta_{x,z}/2$.  Since the theorem accepts the
    87	actual nonnegative error on each fiber, no assumption that a fiber error is at
    88	most one, and no good--bad fiber split, is needed.  One must still formulate
    89	the finite common-extension step that makes the auxiliary space uniform over
    90	$(x,z)$.
    91	
    92	\section{Comparison with the quoted statement}
    93	
    94	Lines~711--725 of
    95	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex} quote the
    96	linearity theorem.  The displayed hypothesis correctly averages over both
    97	group variables.  The displayed conclusion, however, says that the corrected
    98	observable is close for every $u$, whereas Theorem~10 of the cited work gives
    99	closeness only on average over $u$ \cite{Natarajan2017Linearity}.  Moreover,
   100	the provider's equation~(3) proves the bound $\delta$ for binary-measurement
   101	distance; under the operator-distance convention displayed above this is the
   102	bound $2\delta$.  Identifying it with the same bound $\delta$ loses a factor of
   103	two.  The quotation also inserts $\delta\leq1$, which is absent from the
   104	provider theorem and would unnecessarily obstruct applying it with a fiber's
   105	actual defect.  The assertion at the identity follows from exact linearity as
   106	above.
   107	
   108	Lines~825--832 construct the family $O^{x,z,r,s}$ and establish approximate
   109	linearity only after averaging over $x,z,r,r',s,s'$.  They then apply the
   110	single-family theorem separately for every $(x,z)$ and state that sufficiently
   111	many zero ancillas avoid a further extension.  The remaining implicit step is
   112	to make the theorem's possibly fiber-dependent auxiliary spaces uniform.
   113	
   114	The finite setting admits a standard repair.  Apply the theorem on each fiber
   115	with its actual defect, choose one finite auxiliary space large enough for all
   116	returned spaces, and embed each returned space so that its unit vector maps to
   117	one fixed vector.  Extend the conjugated observables by the identity on the
   118	orthogonal complement.  The embeddings may depend on the fiber because the
   119	observables do.  Averaging then yields the conclusion used later in the
   120	chapter.  This is an open reduction, not a counterexample to the quoted theorem
   121	or to the source's eventual combined-measurement conclusion.
   122

   125	Theorem~\path{thm:linearity} and
   126	Remark~\path{rem:linearity-import} in

   132	\path{MIPStarRE/QPBT/Combining/Linearity.lean} assumes a nonnegative defect, a

   137	The companion declaration

   153	
   154	\section{Conclusion}
   155	
   156	The quotation changes averaged closeness to pointwise closeness, inserts an
   157	unnecessary upper bound on $\delta$, and loses a factor of two in translating
   158	binary-measurement distance to operator distance.  Its assertion at the
   159	identity is derivable from exact linearity.  The single-family theorem is now
   160	proved with mean squared operator error at most $2\delta$, equivalently mean
   161	squared binary-measurement error at most $\delta$.  Its use for the family
   162	indexed by $(x,z)$ still requires an explicit finite common-extension argument;
   163	that is the remaining open formal reduction.
